questions.q: What is a threat model?
choices: A list of every known software vulnerability in a system
A model of who your attacker is and what resources they have
A formal proof that a system cannot be breached
A diagram of the network topology an attacker would traverse
questions.explain: A threat model describes who the attacker is (and why they might attack) and what resources they have.

questions.q: An attack that succeeds only 1 time in 1,000,000 can be safely ignored, because attackers won't bother with such poor odds.
questions.explain: We assume the attacker is persistent and lucky: if an attack works 1/1,000,000 times, the attacker will try 1,000,000 times.

questions.q: Which of the following are common assumptions we make about attackers?
choices: They can interact with your systems without anyone noticing
They have general information about your system, such as its OS and potential vulnerabilities
They can coordinate or chain multiple attacks across several systems
They will attack only a single device at a time
They will give up after an attack fails the first time
questions.explain: Attackers are assumed to be stealthy, informed about your system, persistent, willing to spend resources, and able to attack your whole network or chain attacks together.

questions.q: A casino was hacked through a fish-tank thermometer on its network. Which attacker assumption does this illustrate?
choices: Every system is a potential target
Attackers are motivated only by money
Attackers cannot coordinate attacks across systems
Old code is always more secure than new code
questions.explain: Even a seemingly unimportant device can serve as the attacker's way into the network.

questions.q: Why should you be especially careful with old code and old network protocols?
choices: Old code is always written in memory-unsafe languages
Attackers cannot read old code, so its flaws are hard to find
The assumptions it was built on may no longer hold, because the threat model has changed
Old protocols were designed to be insecure on purpose
questions.explain: For example, many early Internet protocols assumed all participants (mostly academics) could be trusted. That assumption no longer holds with billions of devices, some of them malicious.

questions.q: A user keeps clicking "remind me later" on a prompt to restart and finish installing important security updates. What lesson does this illustrate?
choices: Updates should never contain security patches
Security that inconveniences users tends to get put off or bypassed, which leaves the system vulnerable for longer
Users are the attacker in most threat models
Security patches should only be applied by administrators
questions.explain: Users like convenience. If security gets in their way, they will skip it, and the computer stays vulnerable the whole time the update is delayed.

questions.q: As long as a security system is strong enough, it does not matter whether it is user-friendly.
questions.explain: An unusable security system will go unused or be subverted, no matter how secure it is in theory.

questions.q: The NSA's cryptographic equipment stores key material on a token shaped like an ordinary door key, which you insert and turn to activate the device. Why is this a good design?
choices: Physical keys cannot be copied
It makes the cryptography mathematically stronger
It hides the key material from the user
The interface is intuitive, even for people with minimal cryptography training
questions.explain: It is an example of considering human factors: a familiar interface that soldiers in the field can use correctly with little training.

questions.q: What do social engineering attacks exploit?
choices: Bugs in the operating system kernel
Weak cryptographic algorithms
People's trust and access
Race conditions between concurrent processes
questions.explain: Social engineering targets the human element, exploiting other people's trust and access for personal gain.

questions.q: "There is no point putting a $100 lock on a $1 item." What principle does this express?
choices: The expected benefit of a defense should be proportional to the expected cost of the attack
Cheap locks are always sufficient
Security should be designed in from the start
Attackers always target the most valuable item
questions.explain: Security is economics: no system is 100% secure, and how much you spend on defense should match the value at stake.

questions.q: With careful enough engineering, a system can be made 100% secure against all attacks.
questions.explain: No system is completely secure against all attacks. Systems only need protection against a certain level of attack, chosen by cost-benefit analysis.

questions.q: Putting an expensive high-end deadbolt on a screen door is pointless. Which idea does this illustrate?
choices: Fail-safe defaults
Security is only as strong as its weakest link
Separation of responsibility
Shannon's Maxim
questions.explain: Attackers take the path of least resistance. They'll rip through the screen instead of picking the lock, so put your effort into the weakest links.

questions.q: What does the principle of conservative design state?
choices: Systems should use as little code as possible
Systems should be evaluated by their average-case security under typical conditions
Systems should be evaluated by the worst plausible security failure, under assumptions favorable to the attacker
Systems should avoid using new, unproven technologies
questions.explain: If there is any plausible circumstance where the system becomes insecure, it is prudent to consider a more secure system. This is still balanced against security being economics.

questions.q: Safe ratings run from TL-15 (about $3,000) to TL-30 (about $5,000) to TXTL-60 (upwards of $50,000). What do these ratings illustrate?
choices: More security generally costs more, so you must weigh the value of what you protect against what you are willing to pay
Expensive safes cannot be broken into
Safe ratings measure how many attackers a safe can resist
Physical security has nothing to do with computer security
questions.explain: Each rating says how long the safe resists attack (and with which tools). Choosing one is a cost-benefit decision.

questions.q: Under conservative design, you must spend whatever it takes to address every plausible attack scenario, regardless of cost.
questions.explain: Conservative design is balanced against "security is economics." Your threat model decides how much it is worth spending to address a given scenario.

questions.q: Learning that an attack has taken place, as opposed to stopping it or doing something about it, is called:
choices: Prevention
Response
Mediation
Detection
questions.explain: Prevention stops an attack, detection learns that an attack happened, and response does something about it.

questions.q: Detection without response is pointless.
questions.explain: Once you know an attack has happened, you need a way to respond. Otherwise knowing about it accomplishes nothing.

questions.q: Under FIPS 140, Level III devices are meant to be tamper-resistant. What are Level II devices required to be?
choices: Tamper-proof
Tamper-evident, so that tampering is visible (e.g., a broken seal)
Unbypassable
Free of any physical casing
questions.explain: Level II devices only need to show that tampering happened (detection rather than prevention), so they are cheaper and can be used in more applications.

questions.q: Keeping offsite backups of computer systems reflects which part of planning for security?
choices: Response: assume bad things will happen and make sure you can get back to a working state
Prevention: backups stop attacks from happening
Least privilege: backups reduce the privileges of attackers
Complete mediation: backups check every access
questions.explain: Plan for the worst case. Even if a system is completely destroyed, offsite backups let you recover.

questions.q: What is the key idea of defense in depth?
choices: Use one very strong defense instead of several weak ones
Hide the design of the system so attackers can't find weaknesses
Layer multiple types of defenses so an attacker must breach all of them
Give each component only the privileges it needs
questions.explain: As with a castle's walls, moat, and second wall, the attacker has to get through every layer.

questions.q: Two intrusion detectors D1 and D2 are combined in parallel, so either one alerting triggers a response. Compared with using one detector, what happens?
choices: False alarm rate decreases; missed-attack rate increases
False alarm rate increases; missed-attack rate decreases
Both rates decrease
Both rates increase
questions.explain: With either detector able to fire, more real attacks get caught (fewer misses), but each detector's false alarms also trigger responses (more false alarms).

questions.q: Two intrusion detectors D1 and D2 are combined in series, so both must alert to trigger a response. Compared with using one detector, what happens?
choices: False alarm rate decreases; missed-attack rate increases
False alarm rate increases; missed-attack rate decreases
Both rates decrease
Both rates increase
questions.explain: Requiring both to agree filters out false alarms, but an attack missed by either detector now goes unanswered (more misses).

questions.q: Under defense in depth, adding another layer of defense is always worth its cost.
questions.explain: Beware of diminishing returns: if you already have 100 walls, the 101st may not add enough protection to justify its cost (security is economics). Layering is also not foolproof.

questions.q: What does the principle of least privilege say?
choices: Give a program the access privileges it legitimately needs to do its job, and nothing more
Require more than one party to approve any privileged action
Check every access to every object
Run all programs as an unprivileged guest user, regardless of what they need
questions.explain: Each party or component should have exactly as much privilege as its intended role requires.

questions.q: Least privilege reduces the probability that a program will fail or be compromised.
questions.explain: Least privilege doesn't reduce the probability of failure. It reduces the expected cost of failure, because a program with less privilege can do less harm if it goes awry or is subverted.

questions.q: An attacker takes over a program through a buffer overflow. How does least privilege help?
choices: It prevents the buffer overflow from occurring
It detects the overflow and alerts an administrator
The intruder gains only the privileges the program had, so fewer privileges means less harm
It automatically restores the program from a backup
questions.explain: A compromised program is likely fully taken over, so the damage is limited by whatever privileges that program held.

questions.q: Which environment does best at least privilege?
choices: Unix, where each program runs with all of the invoking user's privileges
Windows, where programs run with the user's full privileges
Mobile phones, where each app is sandboxed and usually cannot access other apps' data
None of these differ in least privilege
questions.explain: On Unix and Windows, an editor opened to change one file can read, modify, or delete all of your files. Phone app sandboxing limits the damage a malicious or compromised app can do.

questions.q: A nuclear missile silo requires two launch officers to agree before a launch. Which principle is this?
choices: Least privilege
Separation of responsibility
Fail-safe defaults
Complete mediation
questions.explain: Privilege is split so that no single person has complete power, and more than one party must approve the sensitive action.

questions.q: At a movie theater, one employee sells you a ticket and a different employee tears it and keeps half in a lockbox. What does this mainly protect against?
choices: Counterfeit tickets printed by customers
Customers losing their tickets
Insider fraud: an employee letting friends in without paying
Theater fires blocking the exits
questions.explain: Letting someone in for free would require both employees to collude, which makes the attack harder.

questions.q: Separation of responsibility works because it is more likely that a single party is malicious than that all of several parties are malicious and collude.
questions.explain: Requiring multiple parties to cooperate on a sensitive action means one bad actor is not enough.

questions.q: What does the principle of complete mediation require?
choices: Every user must be mediated by a human administrator
Access control must check every access to every object
Disputes between users must be resolved by a third party
Each access is checked only the first time it occurs
questions.explain: All access must be monitored and protected, with no unchecked paths.

questions.q: What is the name for a single point through which all access must occur, used to ensure complete mediation?
questions.explain: A reference monitor funnels all access through one checkpoint, like an airport security checkpoint.

questions.q: A small number of airport security checkpoints can protect hundreds of gates. What condition must hold for this to work?
choices: Each gate must also have its own checkpoint
Passengers must be screened at random
The checkpoints are handled correctly and there is no way to bypass them
The design of the checkpoints must be kept secret
questions.explain: A reference monitor only works if every access really goes through it and it does its checks correctly.

questions.q: What does Shannon's Maxim state?
choices: The attacker knows the system they are attacking
Every system has at least one vulnerability
Security is only as strong as the weakest link
Longer keys are always more secure
questions.explain: Always assume the attacker knows every detail of the system: its algorithms, hardware, defenses, and so on.

questions.q: Shannon's Maxim implies that open-source applications are necessarily more secure than closed-source applications.
questions.explain: It does not say open source is necessarily more secure. It says not to trust any system that relies on obscurity, and to be skeptical of claims that secret source code makes a system much more secure.

questions.q: Someone argues: "Only 100 people in the world understand this system, so attackers won't bother with it." What is a key flaw in this reasoning?
choices: Obscure systems are always open source
It is self-defeating: if the system becomes popular, attackers have more incentive and obscurity no longer protects it
Obscurity is the strongest form of security
Attackers only target systems with fewer than 100 users
questions.explain: Security through obscurity is brittle and has a poor track record. A motivated attacker can learn the design, and popularity draws attackers.

questions.q: Kerckhoffs's Principle says a cryptographic system should remain secure even when the attacker knows all of its internal details. What is the only thing that should need to be kept secret?
choices: The source code
The encryption algorithm
The hardware design
The secret key
questions.explain: Only the key must stay secret, and the system should make it easy to change keys that are leaked or suspected to be leaked.

questions.q: Why should a system be designed so that only the key is secret and keys are easy to change?
choices: Keys are impossible to leak
If a secret leaks, changing a key is much easier than replacing every running instance of the software
It lets you keep the algorithm secret too
It removes the need for any access control
questions.explain: A leaked key can be swapped out cheaply. A leaked secret design would mean redeploying the system everywhere.

questions.category: Fail-safe defaults and designing security in
questions.q: A default-deny firewall must explicitly decide to forward each packet, or the packet is dropped. What happens if the firewall crashes?
choices: All packets are forwarded, so it fails open
No packets are forwarded, so it fails safe
Only previously seen packets are forwarded
It switches to an allow-all policy until restarted
questions.explain: With default-deny, a failure means nothing gets forwarded. That is secure behavior, which is what fail-safe defaults call for.

questions.category: Fail-safe defaults and designing security in
questions.q: Why is fail-open behavior dangerous for a security mechanism such as a firewall?
choices: It makes the system slower
It makes the system harder to use
An attacker only has to wait for a crash, or cause one, and then everything is let through
It increases the size of the trusted computing base
questions.explain: If failure means "allow," crashing the mechanism becomes an attack.

questions.category: Fail-safe defaults and designing security in
questions.q: Under fail-safe defaults, if a security mechanism fails or crashes, it should default to secure behavior rather than insecure behavior.
questions.explain: That is the definition of fail-safe defaults, balanced against usability when the system goes down.

questions.category: Fail-safe defaults and designing security in
questions.q: Why is it usually hard to retrofit security onto an existing application after it has been specified, designed, and implemented?
choices: You are stuck with the architecture already chosen
You may be unable to decompose the system to get least privilege, complete mediation, defense in depth, and similar properties
Backwards compatibility can force you to keep supporting the insecurities of earlier versions
Security features can only be written in the same language as the original code
questions.explain: Once the architecture is set, good security decompositions may no longer be possible, and backwards compatibility drags old insecurities along.

questions.q: What is the trusted computing base (TCB) of a system?
choices: All of the code that runs on the system
The portion of the system that must operate correctly for the system's security goals to be assured
The set of users who are trusted to log in
The hardware components only
questions.explain: Every TCB component must work correctly. Anything outside the TCB can misbehave, even maliciously, without defeating the security goals.

questions.q: The security goal is that only authorized users can log in to a Linux server over SSH. In a reasonably built system, which components are in the TCB?
choices: The SSH daemon
The operating system
The CPU
A web browser installed on the same machine
questions.explain: The SSH daemon makes the authentication decisions, the OS could tamper with the daemon (e.g., its address space), and the CPU executes its instructions. The OS's memory protection should keep an unprivileged browser from interfering, so the browser is outside the TCB.

questions.q: Which TCB design principle requires that parts of the system outside the TCB cannot modify the TCB's code or state?
choices: Unbypassable (completeness)
Tamper-resistant (security)
Verifiable (correctness)
Least privilege
questions.explain: Tamper-resistance means the TCB's integrity is protected from everyone else.

questions.q: Which TCB design principle says there must be no way to breach system security by going around the TCB?
choices: Unbypassable (completeness)
Tamper-resistant (security)
Verifiable (correctness)
Fail-safe defaults
questions.explain: Unbypassability, or completeness, means all security-relevant activity must go through the TCB.

questions.q: Why does the verifiable (correctness) principle push the TCB to be as simple as possible?
choices: Simple code runs faster
Simple code cannot be attacked
Verifying the correctness of complex subsystems is generally beyond the state of the art
Simple code is easier to keep secret
questions.explain: Only small, simple TCBs can realistically be checked for correctness, hence Keep It Simple, Stupid (KISS).

questions.q: Industry-standard error rates are 1 to 5 defects per thousand lines of code. At the upper end of that range, about how many defects would you expect in a TCB of 100,000 lines?
questions.explain: 5 defects/KLOC x 100 KLOC = 500. A 1,000-line TCB would have only 1 to 5, which is why you should move as much code as possible outside the TCB.

questions.q: A component outside the TCB that behaves maliciously can defeat the system's security goals.
questions.explain: By definition, nothing outside the TCB is relied on. Even if it misbehaves or acts maliciously, it cannot defeat the security goals.

questions.q: What does the advice "decompose for security" mean when designing a system?
choices: Split the system into as many processes as possible for performance
Choose a modular structure based not only on functionality or performance, but so that the TCB is as simple and clear as possible
Put every component in the TCB so that all of it gets audited
Remove all security checks from non-critical modules
questions.explain: A clear separation between the security-critical part (the TCB) and everything else lets you focus effort where it matters and keeps the TCB small.

questions.q: What does the acronym TOCTTOU stand for?
answer: time of check to time of use
questions.explain: Time-Of-Check To Time-Of-Use: the state that was checked changes before it is used.

questions.q: What is the root cause of a TOCTTOU vulnerability?
choices: A buffer overflow in the checking code
The checked state changes between the time it is checked and the time it is used
Using a weak cryptographic key
The attacker knowing the design of the system
questions.explain: It is a race condition: the check is no longer valid by the time the program acts on it.

questions.q: TOCTTOU race conditions are a common failure of which security principle?
choices: Shannon's Maxim
Separation of responsibility
Complete mediation
Defense in depth
questions.explain: TOCTTOU bugs often show up when enforcing access control, such as with a reference monitor. The check no longer covers the access that actually happens.

questions.q: An ATM runs: (1) b := balance, (2) if b < w abort, (3) balance := b - w, (4) dispense w. An attacker can pause one ATM and use a second ATM at the same time. Where should the attacker pause the first ATM to exploit TOCTTOU?
choices: Before step 1
After step 2, before step 3
After step 3, before step 4
After step 4
questions.explain: After step 2 the balance check has passed but the balance hasn't been decremented yet. Withdrawing at another ATM changes the balance, and the paused ATM then acts on the stale value.

questions.q: In the ATM TOCTTOU attack, the account starts with $100. The attacker pauses ATM 1 after its balance check passes, withdraws $100 at ATM 2, then resumes ATM 1 to withdraw $100. How many dollars in total does the attacker receive?
questions.explain: Both ATMs saw a balance of $100 when they checked, so each dispenses $100, for $200 from a $100 account.
